April 27, 2026 2 min read Becton, Dickinson and Company Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD) announced a strategic, non-exclusive collaboration with Suttons Creek to support pharmaceutical and biotech companies in navigating the complexities of combination product development. The partnership brings together BD’s device-agnostic testing capabilities with Suttons Creek’s expertise in combination product development and systems integration. The integrated model is designed to improve coordination across engineering, testing, quality, and regulatory workflows, particularly for biologics, GLP-1 therapies, and other complex drug-device products. According to the announcement, the collaboration aims to address fragmentation across vendor ecosystems by aligning strategy, testing, and delivery considerations earlier in development. This approach is intended to reduce late-stage rework, improve decision-making timelines, and streamline Design History File execution. The companies said customers will benefit from improved integration across development activities, more efficient management of external partners, and continued flexibility in selecting technologies and service providers. The model is also designed to support more predictable development pathways from early-stage planning through clinical and regulatory milestones. The partnership reflects broader industry efforts to improve operational efficiency and reduce risk in the development of increasingly complex combination therapies. Separately, BD has continued to expand its manufacturing footprint, including a $35 million investment to increase prefilled flush syringe production capacity at its Nebraska facility, supporting growing demand for injectable delivery systems. Industry News CordenPharma site passes Brazil’s ANVISA, South Korea’s MFDS GMP inspections The dual regulatory reviews reported zero observations for the CDMO’s highly potent drug manufacturing facility in Plankstadt, Germany. April 24, 2026 2 min read CordenPharma CordenPharma, a contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) headquartered in Basel, Switzerland, announced the successful completion of regulatory inspections by Brazil’s ANVISA and South Korea’s Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) at its Plankstadt, Germany facility. The ANVISA inspection, which focused on the manufacture of a highly potent drug product, concluded ahead of its planned five-day schedule and included a review of manufacturing areas, laboratories, warehouse operations and supporting technical functions, the company said. The MFDS inspection, conducted one week later, also spanned five days and evaluated end-to-end GMP systems for a first-in-class highly potent drug product, including engineering, documentation and operational compliance, according to the CDMO. CordenPharma said both inspections resulted in zero observations, confirming the site’s GMP framework and its ability to manage complex, highly potent manufacturing processes. The company said the outcome supports its containment strategies and operational controls for handling highly potent compounds. The Plankstadt facility’s inspection results come as the company continues to expand its global manufacturing and development footprint. Last month, CordenPharma announced an expansion of its peptide development capabilities in Boulder, Colorado, adding laboratory space to support process development and analytical services alongside its existing peptide API manufacturing operations. The company said the expanded capabilities are intended to improve alignment between development and manufacturing activities and support growing outsourcing demand across its global network. Industry News Ori Biotech, AdAlta, Cell Therapies team on automated cell therapy platform The teaming aims to improve scalability, consistency, and speed for CAR-T and other cell therapy manufacturing in the Asia-Pacific region. April 23, 2026 2 min read Ori Biotech AdAlta, a Melbourne, Australia-based biotechnology company, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Ori Biotech, headquartered in London, and Cell Therapies to deploy Ori Biotech’s automated IRO cell therapy manufacturing platform across the  Asia-Pacific region. According to the announcement, the collaboration aims to address key manufacturing challenges in CAR-T and other cell therapies, including high costs, limited scalability and inconsistent production outcomes. Ori’s IRO platform is reportedly designed to automate and standardize critical steps in cell therapy manufacturing, with targets of 10-50x higher throughput, shorter production timelines, and potential cost reductions of 30-50%. The companies said the platform will be deployed at Cell Therapies for process development and clinical manufacturing, while also supporting optimization of AdAlta’s manufacturing processes to improve scalability and reduce costs. The agreement also seeks to expand manufacturing capacity for additional developers across preclinical, clinical, and commercial programs. AdAlta said the collaboration supports its strategy to deliver scalable and cost-effective cell therapies for solid tumors to global markets, including programs that may benefit from more advanced manufacturing capabilities. Ori’s IRO platform has been used in multiple manufacturing processes and has received an Advanced Manufacturing Technology designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which is intended to support adoption of technologies that improve manufacturing reliability and scalability. The agreement builds on Ori Biotech’s broader efforts to expand adoption of automated manufacturing. Late last year , the company announced a collaboration with Seattle Children’s Research Institute to evaluate the IRO platform’s ability to improve scalability and consistency in cell and gene therapy development. articles.title: How AI is De-Risking Drug Development and Companion Diagnostics
articles.text:
Skip to main content Opinion How AI is De-Risking Drug Development and Companion Diagnostics Digital pathology and artificial intelligence are transforming the drug development landscape, accelerating the path to personalized medicine and better health outcomes. Written by Karan Arora Karan Arora Karan Arora is the Senior Vice President of Advanced Assays, AI, and Pharma Services at Leica Biosystems. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . and Luiza Moore, MD, PhD Luiza Moore, MD, PhD Luiza Moore, MD, PhD, FRCPath is the Global Commercial Product Leader – AI Enabled Assays, at Leica Biosystems. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 12, 2026 | 7 min read Save for Later Companion diagnostics enable more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Image credit: © iStock.com, Yuuji PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Share T he path to bringing a new drug to market is increasingly complex and costly, with development costs now exceeding $2 billion and timelines approaching a decade. 1,2 The stakes have never been higher—demanding new models, new technologies, and new thinking to reduce risk and accelerate breakthroughs. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. This high failure rate has accelerated a shift toward more targeted development strategies. Companion diagnostics are central to this shift, enabling more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3 From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe With over 15 years of experience in diagnostics and pathology, I have seen how “identical” hematoxylin & eosin (H&E) slides can vary across sites—introducing noise, repeat reviews, and delayed decisions. This becomes particularly challenging when variability forces the tissue journey to restart, or worse, necessitates repeat tissue collection from patients, many of whom are critically ill—consuming precious, often irreplaceable patient samples and driving additional trial costs. AI‑enabled tissue quantification has the potential to address these challenges by reducing subjectivity, delivering more reproducible endpoints, and generating cleaner data earlier in drug development. AI can also serve as a second set of eyes during review, helping ensure critical features are not missed and increasing confidence in study outcomes. From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5 These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6 Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support. Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development. In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines. Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment. AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10 As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment. AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate. The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8 When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11 Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights. Collaboration Delivers Greater Value In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed. Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed. Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact. Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact. As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics. He leads a $600M global business unit and 400+ associates at Leica Biosystems, advancing precision oncology through digital pathology, AI, and spatial biology—ensuring patients receive the right treatment the first time. His career spans leadership roles across diagnostics, digital health, and pharmaceuticals, where he has built and scaled organizations that transform the way healthcare is delivered worldwide. At Beckman Coulter, Karan led enterprise strategy, marketing, and market access to accelerate growth. As Chief Commercial Digital Officer at AstraZeneca, he pioneered digital health/data strategies, advanced precision medicine, and launched *AMAZE*, a chronic disease management platform later acquired by Huma. View Full Profile Luiza Moore, MD, PhD Luiza Moore, MD, PhD, FRCPath is a physician-scientist and global leader in oncology diagnostics at Leica Biosystems, focused on digital and computational pathology and the commercialization of innovative diagnostic solutions. With more than 15 years of experience spanning clinical medicine, academia, technology, and biopharma, she brings a unique cross-sector perspective shaped by roles as a practicing pathologist, academic researcher, and industry leader across global technology organizations, health tech startups, and pharmaceutical companies. Her work is focused on advancing precision medicine through the development and real-world deployment of AI-enabled diagnostics at scale. View Full Profile Share You might also be interested in... Share With a Colleague Share This webinar, brought to you by Mission Bio, will be hosted live and available on-demand. Monday, May 11th, 2026 12:00 - 1:00 PM ET Measurable residual disease (MRD) assessment plays a critical role in monitoring acute myeloid leukemia (AML) progression and relapse risk. Current standard-of-care approaches, including multiparameter flow cytometry (MFC) and bulk next-generation sequencing (NGS), can miss phenotypic shifts and rare relapse-driving clones because the results represent averaged cellular populations rather than individual cell behavior. Advances in single-cell multiomic analysis now allow simultaneous evaluation of DNA mutations and cell surface proteins at the resolution of individual cells, enabling deeper disease biology characterization. In this webinar, brought to you by Mission Bio, Zivjena Vucetic, chief medical officer at Mission Bio, present clinical evidence demonstrating how single-cell multiomics improves MRD detection sensitivity and refines relapse prediction in AML. Vucetic examine comparative clinical data, discusses limitations of conventional MRD assays, and highlights how single-cell analysis informs treatment stratification, therapeutic decision making, and future clinical evaluation strategies. Topics to be covered Limitations of current AML MRD assessment methods Comparison of MFC, bulk NGS, and single-cell approaches Detection of rare relapse-driving clones using single-cell multiomics Clinical study results demonstrating improved MRD sensitivity The effect of single-cell MRD analysis on relapse prediction Implications for targeted treatment decisions and clinical trial stratification Zivjena Vucetic, MD, PhD Chief Medical Officer Mission Bio Sponsored by You might also be interested in... Apr 6, 2026 | 3 min read Save for Later Maryam Kazerani Pasikhani studies longitudinal immune monitoring to improve immunotherapy outcomes for patients with cancer. Image credit: Cedars-Sinai Cancer Center, © iStock.com , ediebloom PDF version Share Maryam Kazerani Pasikhani is a postdoctoral researcher at the Cedars-Sinai Cancer Center. Her work encompasses the epigenetic regulation of hematopoiesis and cancer immunology, with a focus on immunotherapeutic strategies for hematologic malignancies. In this Postdoc Portrait interview, she shares why her research matters now and discusses some of the most rewarding aspects of her work. Optimizing Precision Immunotherapy Q | What drew you to hematology and immunology? From as early as I can remember, I have been passionate about finding better treatments for blood cancers. This interest was driven by a desire to serve patients and make a meaningful impact on their lives. That motivation led me to train as a medical laboratory technologist, where examining blood samples and diagnostic tests showed me how early detection can alter the course of hematologic malignancies. Wanting to move from diagnosis to discovery, I pursued a master’s degree in hematology. During my PhD at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, I focused on understanding the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate hematopoietic development. As my training deepened, I became increasingly fascinated by the Nobel Prize-winning immunotherapy and its transformative potential. Leveraging my background in hematology and immunology, I shifted my focus toward optimizing immunotherapeutic strategies for patients with hematologic malignancies. Today, I remain guided by a clear sense of purpose—my “why.” As a cancer researcher, I aim to translate scientific insight into immunotherapeutic approaches that improve outcomes, extend survival, and offer patients lasting hope. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Monitoring Longitudinal Immune Fitness Q | Tell us about your favorite research project and what you’re currently working on. One of my favorite research projects explored how T cell immune fitness changes over time in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This question arose from the observation that several bispecific T cell engager antibodies have not yielded sustained responses in patients with patients. By testing patient-derived T cells against bispecific T cell engager antibodies at different disease stages, I found that T cells exhibit distinct functional states at diagnosis and relapse compared to complete remission. Using an integrated phenotypic, functional, metabolic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic approach, this work provided a mechanistic rationale for moving bispecific antibodies to earlier treatment settings, such as consolidation therapy—particularly in patients in remission with minimal residual disease—where restored T cell function and favorable effector-to-target ratios provide a window of enhanced therapeutic responsiveness and improved clinical outcomes. Building on this work, my current research expands longitudinal immune monitoring to a broader population of patients with cancer on active treatments, including both hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. Using high-dimensional immunophenotyping and activation-induced marker assays, I aim to define T cell immune fitness as a biomarker that can help predict treatment responses and guide more personalized immunotherapy strategies. This large-scale study of approximately 5,000 patient samples is designed to serve as a shared resource for the cancer immunology community. Q | What has been a rewarding aspect of your career so far? The most exciting part of my scientific journey has been seeing how passion, patience, and perseverance have enabled me to conduct high-impact, clinically relevant translational research with the potential to benefit patients with cancer. It has been deeply rewarding to see my work published in leading journals such as Leukemia , Blood , and PNAS , and it was particularly meaningful that two of my favorite projects were recognized with the American Society of Hematology Abstract Achievement Award. These milestones reinforced my commitment to pursuing research that bridges scientific insights and patient care. Equally exciting have been the people I have encountered along the way. Working alongside highly driven scientists who excel professionally while maintaining fulfilling personal lives reshaped how I think about success. I learned that there is no single definition of work-life balance; instead, work-life integration evolves over time. Accepting moments of exhaustion while continuing to move forward with purpose has been an important lesson—one that continues to guide me as a scientist. Q | If you could be a laboratory instrument, which one would you be and why? I would be a fluorescence-activated cell sorter ( FACS ). A FACS machine has the unique ability to bring clarity by resolving heterogeneous cell populations into defined, functional subsets. In many ways, this mirrors my scientific approach—seeking to understand immune diversity rather than averaging it away. Continue reading below... Read More Just as a FACS machine identifies and isolates rare yet meaningful cell populations, my research focuses on uncovering critical immune states that drive treatment response or resistance in patients with cancer. Stratifying cells based on their functional and phenotypic characteristics is central to precision immunotherapy, where identifying the right immune context can determine clinical success. Beyond its technical power, FACS represents rigor, reproducibility, and the translation of complex data into actionable insights. These principles guide my work as I aim to shed light on immune mechanisms and apply them toward more effective and personalized cancer therapies. Responses have been edited for length and clarity. Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support. Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development. In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines. Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment. AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10 As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment. AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate. Collaboration Delivers Greater Value In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed. Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed. Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact. Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact. As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics. Image credit: Cedars-Sinai Cancer Center, © iStock.com , ediebloom PDF version Share Maryam Kazerani Pasikhani is a postdoctoral researcher at the Cedars-Sinai Cancer Center. Her work encompasses the epigenetic regulation of hematopoiesis and cancer immunology, with a focus on immunotherapeutic strategies for hematologic malignancies. In this Postdoc Portrait interview, she shares why her research matters now and discusses some of the most rewarding aspects of her work. Optimizing Precision Immunotherapy Q | What drew you to hematology and immunology? From as early as I can remember, I have been passionate about finding better treatments for blood cancers. This interest was driven by a desire to serve patients and make a meaningful impact on their lives. That motivation led me to train as a medical laboratory technologist, where examining blood samples and diagnostic tests showed me how early detection can alter the course of hematologic malignancies. Wanting to move from diagnosis to discovery, I pursued a master’s degree in hematology. During my PhD at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, I focused on understanding the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate hematopoietic development. As my training deepened, I became increasingly fascinated by the Nobel Prize-winning immunotherapy and its transformative potential. Leveraging my background in hematology and immunology, I shifted my focus toward optimizing immunotherapeutic strategies for patients with hematologic malignancies. Today, I remain guided by a clear sense of purpose—my “why.” As a cancer researcher, I aim to translate scientific insight into immunotherapeutic approaches that improve outcomes, extend survival, and offer patients lasting hope. One of my favorite research projects explored how T cell immune fitness changes over time in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This question arose from the observation that several bispecific T cell engager antibodies have not yielded sustained responses in patients with patients. By testing patient-derived T cells against bispecific T cell engager antibodies at different disease stages, I found that T cells exhibit distinct functional states at diagnosis and relapse compared to complete remission. Using an integrated phenotypic, functional, metabolic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic approach, this work provided a mechanistic rationale for moving bispecific antibodies to earlier treatment settings, such as consolidation therapy—particularly in patients in remission with minimal residual disease—where restored T cell function and favorable effector-to-target ratios provide a window of enhanced therapeutic responsiveness and improved clinical outcomes. Building on this work, my current research expands longitudinal immune monitoring to a broader population of patients with cancer on active treatments, including both hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. Using high-dimensional immunophenotyping and activation-induced marker assays, I aim to define T cell immune fitness as a biomarker that can help predict treatment responses and guide more personalized immunotherapy strategies. This large-scale study of approximately 5,000 patient samples is designed to serve as a shared resource for the cancer immunology community. Q | What has been a rewarding aspect of your career so far? The most exciting part of my scientific journey has been seeing how passion, patience, and perseverance have enabled me to conduct high-impact, clinically relevant translational research with the potential to benefit patients with cancer. It has been deeply rewarding to see my work published in leading journals such as Leukemia , Blood , and PNAS , and it was particularly meaningful that two of my favorite projects were recognized with the American Society of Hematology Abstract Achievement Award. These milestones reinforced my commitment to pursuing research that bridges scientific insights and patient care. Equally exciting have been the people I have encountered along the way. Working alongside highly driven scientists who excel professionally while maintaining fulfilling personal lives reshaped how I think about success. I learned that there is no single definition of work-life balance; instead, work-life integration evolves over time. Accepting moments of exhaustion while continuing to move forward with purpose has been an important lesson—one that continues to guide me as a scientist. Q | If you could be a laboratory instrument, which one would you be and why? I would be a fluorescence-activated cell sorter ( FACS ). Image credit: © iStock.com, Yuuji PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Share T he path to bringing a new drug to market is increasingly complex and costly, with development costs now exceeding $2 billion and timelines approaching a decade. 1,2 The stakes have never been higher—demanding new models, new technologies, and new thinking to reduce risk and accelerate breakthroughs. Up to 90 percent of compounds entering clinical trials never reach the market, often due to unforeseen toxicity or lack of efficacy in heterogenous patient populations. This high failure rate has accelerated a shift toward more targeted development strategies. Companion diagnostics are central to this shift, enabling more precise trials, faster development cycles, and better health outcomes for some of the world’s sickest patients. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape—not only for therapeutics but also for precision diagnostics that guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Digital pathology and AI now sit at the heart of this transformation, offering new ways to extract quantitative biological signals, harmonize global lab variability, and support earlier, sharper decision‑making in clinical trials. 3 From Failure to Focus: Reducing Drug Development Risk with Computational Pathology Biology is heterogeneous, traditional pathology is variable, and global clinical trial operations introduce noise that can obscure early efficacy or safety signals. 4 Whole‑slide imaging (WSI) and computational pathology have the potential to directly address these challenges by scaling objective readouts from tissue and associated morphology with clinical outcomes. This becomes particularly challenging when variability forces the tissue journey to restart, or worse, necessitates repeat tissue collection from patients, many of whom are critically ill—consuming precious, often irreplaceable patient samples and driving additional trial costs. AI‑enabled tissue quantification has the potential to address these challenges by reducing subjectivity, delivering more reproducible endpoints, and generating cleaner data earlier in drug development. AI can also serve as a second set of eyes during review, helping ensure critical features are not missed and increasing confidence in study outcomes. From Slides to Quantitative Biomarkers Modern AI models are capable of identifying subtle morphologic patterns that correlate with prognosis, molecular status, and treatment response. For example, multiple‑instance learning (MIL)-based approaches have matured to clinical‑grade performance for predicting histology-derived endpoints, providing objective, reproducible metrics appropriate for global deployment and regulatory evaluation. 5 These biomarkers further reduce biological uncertainty by enabling earlier biological signal detection and quantitative features that can be deployed consistently across global trials. This shift allows development teams to detect trends long before traditional clinical endpoints mature. 6 Strengthening Oncology Trial Decisions Through Early AI‑Enabled Signal Detection AI‑enabled biomarkers support early patient stratification, reduce biological and operational noise, and enable more accurate response prediction across oncology trials . Increasingly, studies demonstrate that morphology‑derived signatures extracted from routine histology can predict outcomes and drug response earlier—and often more reproducibly—than traditional clinical readouts. 6 This is particularly relevant in immuno‑oncology, where response to therapy is shaped by both tumor-intrinsic features and the tumor microenvironment. While established biomarkers such as PD‑L1 immunohistochemistry have been central to patient selection, they only capture part of this biological complexity. In this context, weakly supervised AI models applied to standard H&E sections can infer tumor microenvironment characteristics and immunotherapy response at scale, complementing PD-L1 based strategies and enabling earlier enrichment and informed decisions for treatment optimization. 3,6 Bridging the R&D–to–Real‑World Gap in CDx Development Companion diagnostics (CDx) failures often occur not during discovery, but at deployment—when real‑world laboratory variability undermines analytical performance. Multi‑center datasets consistently demonstrate significant inter-laboratory variation in staining and scanning, driving domain shift and degrading model performance unless proactively managed. 7 Recent studies underscore how stain‑normalization techniques are evolving to address this challenge. Methods such as Macenko, Reinhard, and Vahadane continue to serve as strong and reliable baselines, sustaining their role as workhorses in digital pathology workflows. In parallel, generative adversarial network‑based and hybrid approaches are demonstrating clear advantages in cross‑site robustness, enabling models to generalize more effectively across heterogeneous scanners and staining protocols. Most notably, techniques, such as stain‑aware normalization and Beer–Lambert-based models, offer substantial reductions in performance loss under shifting staining conditions, representing a meaningful advance toward more resilient and deployment‑ready image analysis pipelines. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8 Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions. Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery. Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness. In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support. Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development. In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines. Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment. AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10 As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment. AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate. The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8 When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11 Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights. Collaboration Delivers Greater Value In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed. Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed. Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact. Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact. As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics. These capabilities are critical for achieving analytically valid CDx deployment across global laboratory networks. 8
8
Infrastructure Readiness: Cloud‑Native, Compliant, and Audit‑Ready
Digital pathology infrastructure continues to mature globally, with cloud‑native, compliant, and fully auditable platforms emerging as the foundation for scalable deployment. The FDA clearance of WSI for primary diagnosis has further facilitated adoption, enabling clinical‑grade digital pathology infrastructure to operate reliably and securely across institutions.
Importantly, the infrastructure readiness in AI-enabled pathology extends beyond software and cloud architecture to the full end-to-end system, from tissue handling to computational analysis. At present, glass slides remain the biological ground truth, supporting regulatory review, retrospective analysis, and future biomarker discovery.
Not all whole-slide scanners are equivalent in optical quality, color fidelity, throughput, or reproducibility. These differences can have a significant impact on downstream algorithm performance if not carefully controlled. As AI-derived endpoints move into registrational trials and companion diagnostic deployment, the selection of clinically validated, high-performance scanning platforms become a critical component of infrastructure readiness.
In parallel, regulatory expectations for AI in healthcare are becoming increasingly well defined, with greater emphasis on adherence to Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP), transparency in AI‑generated outputs, and robust oversight across the total product lifecycle—including proactive post‑market monitoring.  For AI-enabled assays, this includes controls such as cell line and reference material controls, locked models, cross-lab performance monitoring, and auditable data lineage. Cloud‑native pipelines, designed to meet HIPAA/GDPR requirements, can now offer essential capabilities such as comprehensive audit trails, encryption, role‑based access control, and data lineage. Together, these developments support deployment-ready, regulator-aligned digital pathology workflows for next-generation companion diagnostics and clinical decision support.
Regional CDx Regulatory Landscape
In the US, the FDA provides relatively clear CDx co‑development pathways , supported by oncology‑focused pilot programs that encourage early alignment between therapeutic and diagnostic development.
CDx co‑development pathways
In Europe, the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR) elevates CDx to Class C, requiring Notified Body review and consultation with the European Medicines Agency . While this shift strengthens regulatory rigor and oversight, it also introduces increased workload, operational complexity, and longer development timelines.
European Medicines Agency
Comparative analyses show widening differences between FDA and IVDR requirements—underscoring the importance of coordinated, early regulatory planning. Without proactive alignment, these regional differences can introduce delays, rework, and downstream risk to global CDx deployment.
AI Augmenting Pathologists Workflows
AI has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, standardization, and efficiency in pathology. However, contextual interpretation, clinical judgement, and patient‑impacting decisions remain firmly within the expertise of the pathologist. Reviews continue to emphasize that safe and effective use of AI requires clinician‑in‑the‑loop workflows, where human oversight is integral to decision‑making. 9,10
9,10
As a cyto- and histopathologist, I have spent countless hours performing manual, time‑intensive tasks such as accurately counting inflammatory cells to diagnose acute bladder inflammation or enumerating mitotic figures to determine breast cancer grade, decisions that directly influence patient treatment.
AI has the potential to relieve pathologists of these repetitive, low-value tasks, allowing us to focus on integrative reasoning, clinical context, and complex diagnostic synthesis—capabilities that algorithms cannot replicate.
The Future: Multimodal, Generalizable, and Equitable
Next‑generation multimodal foundation models integrate histology with clinical reports, genomics, and proteomics to improve disease classification, survival prediction, and biological interpretability across cancer types. These models move beyond single‑modality analysis, enabling richer context and more biologically meaningful insights. 8
When rigorously validated across sites and paired with stain‑robust deployment‑ready pipelines, these systems have the potential to expand access to precision diagnostics globally, including in low‑resource settings where specialist expertise and advanced infrastructure may be limited. 3,11
3,11
Importantly, AI is not a substitute for skilled laboratory staff and researchers; rather it serves as a powerful second set of eyes—enhancing precision, increasing agility, and elevating the quality of scientific work with deeper insights.
Collaboration Delivers Greater Value
In an environment where accelerating time‑to‑market is increasingly critical, building diagnostics capabilities from scratch can introduce unnecessary cost, delay, and execution risk. Strategic collaboration offers a more efficient path forward, allowing innovation to scale without sacrificing rigor or speed.
Beyond operational efficiency, collaboration also enables a departure from traditional CDx partnership models that often constrain speed and flexibility. Emerging platform-based, data-centric approaches allow therapeutic and diagnostic development to progress in parallel, reducing hand-offs, compressing timelines, and enabling faster launches. Importantly, these models support earlier alignment on evidence generation, regulatory strategy, and global deployment—reducing late-stage friction that has historically delayed market entry. Partnerships are helping build comprehensive antibody libraries, powered by sophisticated AI analysis. Instead of starting anew, pharmaceutical companies can leverage robust, pre‑validated datasets to establish proof‑of‑concept more rapidly and with greater confidence. For emerging biomarkers, the platform’s ability to generate custom antibodies on demand adds critical flexibility and speed.
Looking Ahead: A New Model for Evidence Generation
As personalized medicine becomes the standard of care, the pressure on pharmaceutical companies to develop robust companion diagnostics has never been greater—elevating risk mitigation capabilities from operational considerations to sources of competitive advantage. AI is emerging as the new scientific lens for drug development and CDx. By reducing biological uncertainty, harmonizing variability across global laboratory networks, and supporting earlier, more confident decision‑making, AI is accelerating the path from discovery to meaningful patient impact.
Critically, the next evolution of evidence generation will integrate real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trial data. When combined with AI-enabled diagnostics, RWE enables ongoing validation of biomarker performance across more diverse patient populations, strengthening confidence in clinical utility beyond controlled trials. This approach allows best practices to be scaled more rapidly, accelerating the translation of approved innovations into meaningful patient impact.
As cloud‑based pathology infrastructure continues to mature and regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics evolve, these technologies will increasingly define how evidence is generated, validated, and translated into the next generation of precision therapeutics.

Apr 6, 2026 | 3 min read Save for Later Maryam Kazerani Pasikhani studies longitudinal immune monitoring to improve immunotherapy outcomes for patients with cancer. Image credit: Cedars-Sinai Cancer Center, © iStock.com , ediebloom PDF version Share Maryam Kazerani Pasikhani is a postdoctoral researcher at the Cedars-Sinai Cancer Center. Her work encompasses the epigenetic regulation of hematopoiesis and cancer immunology, with a focus on immunotherapeutic strategies for hematologic malignancies. In this Postdoc Portrait interview, she shares why her research matters now and discusses some of the most rewarding aspects of her work. Optimizing Precision Immunotherapy Q | What drew you to hematology and immunology? From as early as I can remember, I have been passionate about finding better treatments for blood cancers. This interest was driven by a desire to serve patients and make a meaningful impact on their lives. That motivation led me to train as a medical laboratory technologist, where examining blood samples and diagnostic tests showed me how early detection can alter the course of hematologic malignancies. Wanting to move from diagnosis to discovery, I pursued a master’s degree in hematology. During my PhD at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, I focused on understanding the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate hematopoietic development. As my training deepened, I became increasingly fascinated by the Nobel Prize-winning immunotherapy and its transformative potential. Leveraging my background in hematology and immunology, I shifted my focus toward optimizing immunotherapeutic strategies for patients with hematologic malignancies. Today, I remain guided by a clear sense of purpose—my “why.” As a cancer researcher, I aim to translate scientific insight into immunotherapeutic approaches that improve outcomes, extend survival, and offer patients lasting hope. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Monitoring Longitudinal Immune Fitness Q | Tell us about your favorite research project and what you’re currently working on. One of my favorite research projects explored how T cell immune fitness changes over time in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This question arose from the observation that several bispecific T cell engager antibodies have not yielded sustained responses in patients with patients. By testing patient-derived T cells against bispecific T cell engager antibodies at different disease stages, I found that T cells exhibit distinct functional states at diagnosis and relapse compared to complete remission. Using an integrated phenotypic, functional, metabolic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic approach, this work provided a mechanistic rationale for moving bispecific antibodies to earlier treatment settings, such as consolidation therapy—particularly in patients in remission with minimal residual disease—where restored T cell function and favorable effector-to-target ratios provide a window of enhanced therapeutic responsiveness and improved clinical outcomes. Building on this work, my current research expands longitudinal immune monitoring to a broader population of patients with cancer on active treatments, including both hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. Using high-dimensional immunophenotyping and activation-induced marker assays, I aim to define T cell immune fitness as a biomarker that can help predict treatment responses and guide more personalized immunotherapy strategies. This large-scale study of approximately 5,000 patient samples is designed to serve as a shared resource for the cancer immunology community. Q | What has been a rewarding aspect of your career so far? The most exciting part of my scientific journey has been seeing how passion, patience, and perseverance have enabled me to conduct high-impact, clinically relevant translational research with the potential to benefit patients with cancer. It has been deeply rewarding to see my work published in leading journals such as Leukemia , Blood , and PNAS , and it was particularly meaningful that two of my favorite projects were recognized with the American Society of Hematology Abstract Achievement Award. These milestones reinforced my commitment to pursuing research that bridges scientific insights and patient care. Equally exciting have been the people I have encountered along the way. Working alongside highly driven scientists who excel professionally while maintaining fulfilling personal lives reshaped how I think about success. I learned that there is no single definition of work-life balance; instead, work-life integration evolves over time. Accepting moments of exhaustion while continuing to move forward with purpose has been an important lesson—one that continues to guide me as a scientist. Q | If you could be a laboratory instrument, which one would you be and why? I would be a fluorescence-activated cell sorter ( FACS ). A FACS machine has the unique ability to bring clarity by resolving heterogeneous cell populations into defined, functional subsets. In many ways, this mirrors my scientific approach—seeking to understand immune diversity rather than averaging it away. Continue reading below... Image credit: Cedars-Sinai Cancer Center, © iStock.com , ediebloom PDF version Share Maryam Kazerani Pasikhani is a postdoctoral researcher at the Cedars-Sinai Cancer Center. Her work encompasses the epigenetic regulation of hematopoiesis and cancer immunology, with a focus on immunotherapeutic strategies for hematologic malignancies. In this Postdoc Portrait interview, she shares why her research matters now and discusses some of the most rewarding aspects of her work. Optimizing Precision Immunotherapy Q | What drew you to hematology and immunology? From as early as I can remember, I have been passionate about finding better treatments for blood cancers. This interest was driven by a desire to serve patients and make a meaningful impact on their lives. That motivation led me to train as a medical laboratory technologist, where examining blood samples and diagnostic tests showed me how early detection can alter the course of hematologic malignancies. Wanting to move from diagnosis to discovery, I pursued a master’s degree in hematology. During my PhD at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, I focused on understanding the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate hematopoietic development. As my training deepened, I became increasingly fascinated by the Nobel Prize-winning immunotherapy and its transformative potential. Leveraging my background in hematology and immunology, I shifted my focus toward optimizing immunotherapeutic strategies for patients with hematologic malignancies. Today, I remain guided by a clear sense of purpose—my “why.” As a cancer researcher, I aim to translate scientific insight into immunotherapeutic approaches that improve outcomes, extend survival, and offer patients lasting hope. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Monitoring Longitudinal Immune Fitness Q | Tell us about your favorite research project and what you’re currently working on. One of my favorite research projects explored how T cell immune fitness changes over time in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This question arose from the observation that several bispecific T cell engager antibodies have not yielded sustained responses in patients with patients. By testing patient-derived T cells against bispecific T cell engager antibodies at different disease stages, I found that T cells exhibit distinct functional states at diagnosis and relapse compared to complete remission. Using an integrated phenotypic, functional, metabolic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic approach, this work provided a mechanistic rationale for moving bispecific antibodies to earlier treatment settings, such as consolidation therapy—particularly in patients in remission with minimal residual disease—where restored T cell function and favorable effector-to-target ratios provide a window of enhanced therapeutic responsiveness and improved clinical outcomes. Building on this work, my current research expands longitudinal immune monitoring to a broader population of patients with cancer on active treatments, including both hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. Using high-dimensional immunophenotyping and activation-induced marker assays, I aim to define T cell immune fitness as a biomarker that can help predict treatment responses and guide more personalized immunotherapy strategies. This large-scale study of approximately 5,000 patient samples is designed to serve as a shared resource for the cancer immunology community. Q | What has been a rewarding aspect of your career so far? The most exciting part of my scientific journey has been seeing how passion, patience, and perseverance have enabled me to conduct high-impact, clinically relevant translational research with the potential to benefit patients with cancer. It has been deeply rewarding to see my work published in leading journals such as Leukemia , Blood , and PNAS , and it was particularly meaningful that two of my favorite projects were recognized with the American Society of Hematology Abstract Achievement Award. These milestones reinforced my commitment to pursuing research that bridges scientific insights and patient care. Equally exciting have been the people I have encountered along the way. Working alongside highly driven scientists who excel professionally while maintaining fulfilling personal lives reshaped how I think about success. I learned that there is no single definition of work-life balance; instead, work-life integration evolves over time. Accepting moments of exhaustion while continuing to move forward with purpose has been an important lesson—one that continues to guide me as a scientist. Q | If you could be a laboratory instrument, which one would you be and why? I would be a fluorescence-activated cell sorter ( FACS ). A FACS machine has the unique ability to bring clarity by resolving heterogeneous cell populations into defined, functional subsets. In many ways, this mirrors my scientific approach—seeking to understand immune diversity rather than averaging it away. Continue reading below... Stratifying cells based on their functional and phenotypic characteristics is central to precision immunotherapy, where identifying the right immune context can determine clinical success. Beyond its technical power, FACS represents rigor, reproducibility, and the translation of complex data into actionable insights. These principles guide my work as I aim to shed light on immune mechanisms and apply them toward more effective and personalized cancer therapies. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.
